Divorce

precepts.text: What God hath joined together, let not man put asunder; Moses suffered divorce for the hardness of your hearts, but from the beginning it was not so.
precepts.point: Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery; and whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
Christ magnified this law. The Pharisees came tempting him: “Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for every cause?” He answered from the beginning: “he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”

Then they asked the question that brings in the bill of divorcement: “Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement, and to put her away?” And he said, “Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.” The writing of divorcement given in her hand was suffered because of the hardness of hearts; it was not so from the beginning.

Then Christ set the bound on it: “Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery: and whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery.”

precepts.text: If a man put away his wife and she become another man's, shall he return unto her again? shall not that land be greatly polluted?
precepts.point: The question is whether a woman who leaves her husband and becomes another man's wife can be joined to the first again; the prophet asks the same thing: shall he return unto her again? shall not that land be greatly polluted?

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
The question is whether a woman who leaves her husband and becomes another man's wife can be joined to the first again. The law answers: “Her former husband, which sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled; for that is abomination before the Lord: and thou shalt not cause the land to sin”.

The prophet asks the same thing out of this law: “They say, If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and become another man’s, shall he return unto her again? shall not that land be greatly polluted?” The land greatly polluted in Jeremiah is the land caused to sin here; the answer to his question is this law, and it is no.

precepts.text: Thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.
precepts.point: The war laws give the same understanding: the man that had betrothed a wife and not taken her was sent back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her, for the Lord is the one that goeth with the host to fight against the enemies.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
“When a man hath taken a new wife, he shall not go out to war, neither shall he be charged with any business: but he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken.” Make it plain: the first year, stay at home and make a baby.

Genesis lays the ground of the marriage he stays home for: “Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.” Her desire is to her husband, and he rules over her; the year free at home is given to that.

precepts.text: Let every man have his own wife, and let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence, and likewise also the wife unto the husband.
precepts.point: The war laws give the same understanding: the man that had betrothed a wife and not taken her was sent back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her, for the Lord is the one that goeth with the host to fight against the enemies.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
“Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband. Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband.”

Husband and wife render due benevolence to one another; benevolence means good, it is a good thing. The year free at home to cheer up his wife is that benevolence rendered: every man with his own wife, every woman with her own husband, each giving the other what is due. Stay at home the first year and make a baby.

precepts.text: When thou goest out to battle, be not afraid, for the Lord thy God is with thee.
precepts.point: The war laws give the same understanding: the man that had betrothed a wife and not taken her was sent back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her, for the Lord is the one that goeth with the host to fight against the enemies.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
The war laws give the same understanding as the new wife's year at home. “When thou goest out to battle against thine enemies, and seest horses, and chariots, and a people more than thou, be not afraid of them: for the Lord thy God is with thee, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.”

The Lord is the one with the host when it goes to battle; the battle does not hang on the one man newly married. So he is not sent out to war, and is not charged with any business; he is free at home one year.

precepts.text: The Lord your God is he that goeth with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you.
precepts.point: The war laws give the same understanding: the man that had betrothed a wife and not taken her was sent back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her, for the Lord is the one that goeth with the host to fight against the enemies.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
“For the Lord your God is he that goeth with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you.” Because the Lord is the one that goeth with the host to fight against the enemies, men could be sent home before the battle.

“What man is there that hath built a new house, and hath not dedicated it? let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man dedicate it.” The man with a new house is sent back, and the same words send back the man that had betrothed a wife. It is the same understanding as the new husband not going out to war: the Lord fights, and the man is kept for his house and his wife.

precepts.text: What man hath betrothed a wife and not taken her? let him go and return unto his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her.
precepts.point: The war laws give the same understanding: the man that had betrothed a wife and not taken her was sent back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her, for the Lord is the one that goeth with the host to fight against the enemies.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
“And what man is there that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her? let him go and return unto his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man take her.” The war laws give the same understanding as this law.

The man that had betrothed a wife and not taken her was sent back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her; the man that has taken a new wife shall not go out to war at all, but be free at home one year to cheer up his wife. Both stand on the same ground: the Lord is the one that goeth with the host to fight against the enemies, so the man is not needed at the battle and is kept for his wife.

precepts.text: The people gathered the manna and ground it in mills, or beat it in a mortar, and made cakes of it.
precepts.point: Taking a man's tool takes away his living, like somebody stealing your tools so you cannot make a living. It is better that they steal your money, because with your tools you can go back and make more money.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
What is the millstone? A tool for grinding meal. “And the people went about, and gathered it, and ground it in mills, or beat it in a mortar, and baked it in pans, and made cakes of it”. The manna was gathered and ground in mills or beaten in a mortar and baked into cakes; that is the work of the nether and the upper millstone.

No man shall take the millstone to pledge, “for he taketh a man’s life to pledge”: take the mill, and the man cannot grind his meal or make his bread.

precepts.text: He that taketh away his neighbour's living slayeth him.
precepts.point: Taking a man's tool takes away his living, like somebody stealing your tools so you cannot make a living. It is better that they steal your money, because with your tools you can go back and make more money.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
“No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man’s life to pledge.” Ecclesiasticus says how a tool is a man's life: “He that taketh away his neighbour’s living slayeth him; and he that defraudeth the labourer of his hire is a bloodshedder.”

Taking a man's tool takes away his living, like somebody stealing your tools so you cannot make a living. It is better that they steal your money, because with your tools you can go back and make more money; take the tools and the living is gone. That is why the millstone taken to pledge is a man's life taken to pledge.

precepts.text: Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married.
precepts.point: The Lord said, if her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? Had her father chastised her and rebuked her sharply, she would not have had that tongue. That is for a lot of our sisters today who do not have that understanding.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
“Remember what the Lord thy God did unto Miriam by the way, after that ye were come forth out of Egypt.” Here is what happened by the way: “And Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married: for he had married an Ethiopian woman.”

Miriam was not supposed to be speaking against Moses. That speaking is what brought on her what the Lord did unto her.

precepts.text: The anger of the Lord was kindled, the cloud departed from off the tabernacle, and Miriam became leprous, white as snow.
precepts.point: The Lord said, if her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? Had her father chastised her and rebuked her sharply, she would not have had that tongue. That is for a lot of our sisters today who do not have that understanding.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
What the Lord did unto Miriam: “And the anger of the Lord was kindled against them; and he departed. And the cloud departed from off the tabernacle; and, behold, Miriam became leprous, white as snow: and Aaron looked upon Miriam, and, behold, she was leprous.”

For speaking against Moses, the anger of the Lord was kindled, the cloud departed from off the tabernacle, and Miriam became leprous, white as snow. That is what Israel is told to remember by the way.

precepts.text: If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days?
precepts.point: The Lord said, if her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? Had her father chastised her and rebuked her sharply, she would not have had that tongue. That is for a lot of our sisters today who do not have that understanding.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
“And the Lord said unto Moses, If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? let her be shut out from the camp seven days, and after that let her be received in again.”

Had her father chastised her and rebuked her sharply, she would not have had that tongue to speak against Moses. That is for a lot of our sisters today who do not have that understanding. Remember what the Lord did unto Miriam.

precepts.text: If thou take thy neighbour's raiment to pledge, deliver it by that the sun goeth down, for that is his covering only.
precepts.point: The history shows how wicked we were to each other: Israel laid themselves down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar, stacking up people's raiment like pallets and drinking the wine of the condemned in the house of their god, instead of returning the pledge before the sun went down as righteousness. That is why the Lord was judging us.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
The law of the poor man's pledge was already given: “If thou at all take thy neighbour’s raiment to pledge, thou shalt deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down: For that is his covering only, it is his raiment for his skin: wherein shall he sleep? and it shall come to pass, when he crieth unto me, that I will hear; for I am gracious.”

That is the same word as “In any case thou shalt deliver him the pledge again when the sun goeth down, that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee”. His raiment is his covering only; keep it overnight and he has nothing to sleep in, and when he crieth unto the Most High, he will hear, for he is gracious. Return it by sundown and he blesses thee instead, and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the Lord thy God.

precepts.text: For three transgressions of Israel and for four: they lay themselves down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar.
precepts.point: The history shows how wicked we were to each other: Israel laid themselves down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar, stacking up people's raiment like pallets and drinking the wine of the condemned in the house of their god, instead of returning the pledge before the sun went down as righteousness. That is why the Lord was judging us.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
The history shows how wicked we were to each other with this very law. “Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes”. And among the four: “they lay themselves down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar, and they drink the wine of the condemned in the house of their god.”

Instead of returning the pledge before the sun went down as righteousness, Israel laid themselves down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar, stacking up people's raiment like pallets, and drinking the wine of the condemned in the house of their god. The poor man was to sleep in his own raiment and bless thee; instead Israel slept on it. That is why the Lord was judging us.

precepts.text: Amaziah slew his father's murderers, but their children he slew not, according to that which is written in the book of the law of Moses.
precepts.point: The soul that sinneth, it shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
The law applied by a king. “And it came to pass, as soon as the kingdom was confirmed in his hand, that he slew his servants which had slain the king his father. But the children of the murderers he slew not: according unto that which is written in the book of the law of Moses, wherein the Lord commanded, saying, The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor the children be put to death for the fathers; but every man shall be put to death for his own sin.”

Amaziah slew his father's murderers, but their children he slew not, because this law is written in the book of the law of Moses. The murderers died for their own sin; their children had not done it, so they were not put to death.

precepts.text: The soul that sinneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.
precepts.point: The soul that sinneth, it shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
“The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.”

That is this law in the prophet: every man put to death for his own sin, and no other man's. The son does not carry the father's iniquity, nor the father the son's; each man's righteousness or wickedness is upon himself.

precepts.text: Her former husband may not take her again to be his wife after she is defiled, for that is abomination and causes the land to sin.
precepts.point: By the law, a woman who is put away and becomes another man's is defiled to her former husband, and taking her back defiles the land. The Most High does not permit it, but with no king in the land and no enforcement of the law, this is what men did.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

precepts.why: “Her former husband, which sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled; for that is abomination before the Lord: and thou shalt not cause the land to sin”. The Levite going after his concubine to bring her again was the very thing the law forbids. Taking a woman back after she is defiled to her former husband is abomination and causes the land to sin; the Most High does not permit it. But there was no king in the land and no enforcement of the law, and this is what men did, with the damsel’s father rejoicing to meet him.

precepts.text: The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor children for the fathers; every man shall be put to death for his own sin.
precepts.point: When the kingdom was confirmed, he slew the servants who had killed his father, but did not slay their children, according to the law of Moses that every man is put to death for his own sin.

note.label: 2 Kings 14: Amaziah, the Imperfect Heart, and Jeroboam II

precepts.why:
“The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin.”

When the kingdom was confirmed in his hand, Amaziah slew the servants who had slain the king his father. “But the children of the murderers he slew not”, because this is the law of Moses. Kings quotes it word for word from the book of the law. Every man is put to death for his own sin.

precepts.text: Every man shall be put to death for his own sin, not for the sin of his father or his child.
precepts.point: He slew the murderers but he did not slay their children, because it is written in the law of Moses that the fathers shall not die for the children, nor the children for the fathers, but every man shall die for his own sin. This is a foundational law: a man answers for his own sin, not for another man's.

note.label: 2 Chronicles 25: Amaziah Serves the Most High With a Divided Heart

precepts.why:
This is the law Amaziah followed, straight from Moses: “The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin.”

It is a foundational law. A man answers for his own sin, not for the sin of his father or his child. That is why Amaziah slew the servants that killed the king his father, “But he slew not their children”, doing “as it is written in the law in the book of Moses.”

precepts.text: The bill of divorcement Moses allowed, given into her hand when he sent her out of his house.
precepts.point: The trouble in that day was men finding any cause at all to put a woman away. Whosoever putteth away his wife, except it be for fornication, and marrieth another, committeth adultery, and puts her into sin as well.

note.label: Matthew 19: Marriage, the Young Man's Possessions, and the Twelve Thrones

precepts.why:
“Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement, and to put her away?” “Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.”

This is the bill of divorcement Moses allowed: “When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house.” It was written for some uncleanness found in her, given into her hand when he sent her out of his house, and it was suffered because of the hardness of their hearts.

The trouble in that day was men finding any cause at all to put a woman away. Christ brings it back to the beginning: “Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery: and whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery.” The man who puts her away for anything but fornication and marries another commits adultery, and he puts her into sin as well, because whoever marries her commits adultery too.

points: A man with a new wife shall not go to war nor be charged with business, but be free at home one year and cheer up his wife: your wife is depressed because you do not cheer her up.

Cheering her up begins with giving her a baby and the act of it, and it continues through the pregnancy and the difficulties after: after the eighty days of the second child he left the kids with Deacon Malachi's household and took his wife to the Poconos.

Take her out from time to time; help as much as you can, because the grandmother and the sisters who used to surround a new mother are not there and it is often the two of you alone; that stretch is a strain on her.

note.label: Restoring the Broken Minds of the Daughters of Zion

points: Ancient weddings were an agreement between families, a celebration, and a marriage feast. The twentieth century made it an industry: jewelry, dresses, venues, photography, catering, decorations, bachelor and bachelorette parties, rehearsal dinners, DJs. The covenant becomes a wedding event, people marry for the party, and a seventy-five-thousand-dollar package with a smoke-and-lights elevator entrance is a down payment on a house or seed money for a business. If it were really about being together you would just go and do it. You spend more time planning one day than preparing for a lifetime.

When a man hath taken a new wife, he shall not go out to war, neither be charged with any business; he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife. Not a honeymoon vacation but a year of responsibility to establish the household, bring down seed, and stabilize the family. Deuteronomy 20:7 sends the betrothed man home from the battle lest another man take her. The honeymoon says vacation and romantic escape; the Bible says stay home and build.

Taking your wife on a trip or a date every time there is turmoil pretends nothing is wrong for a day or two, and the elephant in the room comes back. A brother who rewarded his wife's behaviour with vacations for years recently had her come through the window and punch him in the face. Ask yourself: if marriage originated with God, why do people learn it from movies? If culture defines it by romance, why does scripture define it by responsibility?

The example: as soon as the kingdom was confirmed in Amaziah's hand, he slew his servants which had slain the king his father, but the children of the murderers he slew not, according unto that which is written in the book of the law of Moses.
The soul that sinneth, it shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.
